coder_notes: TORN CALL ON THE CENTRAL CONSTRUCT: the data are unambiguously video-derived (46 ERA videos x 150 frames + 2 FLAME videos, one contributing 2,003 annotated frames) and the model consumes adjacent frames F(n-2), F(n), F(n+2); flip augmentation is applied before '80% to train and 20% to test'. If that division were frame-random, leakage would be high. But the paper never says HOW the division was made, so split_protocol = not_reported and leakage_risk = medium (the conservative code); a coder who treats 'divided 80/20' as implying a random frame split would code random_resplit + high. (2) n_train/n_val/n_test not_reported: only percentages and per-source video/frame counts are given, no split counts; there is no validation set. (3) class_balance_reported coded `yes` on the video-level fire/non-fire composition (20 of 46 ERA videos); no pixel-level class balance is given, although a combined BCE+dice loss is used 'to reduce the impacts of class imbalance'. (4) adverse_weather_tested coded `yes` but the fog is SYNTHETIC (algorithmically generated corruption), not real weather. (5) tested_unseen_site_or_season coded `yes` via the Corsican Fire cross-dataset test (different locations, never trained on). Cross-dataset delta: IoU 0.868 -> 0.848 (-2.0 pts), accuracy 97.9% -> 94.89% (-3.0 pts). (6) The 14.12 ms / 66.13 FPS inference figure is desktop-GPU latency, not an ignition-to-alarm time, so time_to_detection = not_reported.

coder_notes: KEY LEAKAGE FINDING: the split is explicitly taken over the AUGMENTED pool. 7,000 images -> 1,000 dropped -> 6,000 -> each image rotated 90/180/270 deg -> 24,000, and 'our dataset is divided as follows: 70% for training images, 10% for test images, and 20% for validation images'. Rotated copies of the same source image are therefore near-certain to appear on both sides -> leakage_risk = high. TORN CALLS: (1) task coded `detection_bbox` (YOLOv8 + TranSDet small-object detection), but the paper labels images into two classes (fire / non-fire), stores per-image JSON annotations, and reports only classification-style metrics (training/testing accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure; no mAP and no IoU) — `classification` is a strong alternative and this is my least confident task code in the set. (2) comparison_is_like_for_like coded `unclear` rather than `no`: 'Table 6 shows recently published fire detection models with precision, recall, and FM' reads as literature-sourced numbers under other protocols (note ResNet's recall of 98.6% exceeds the authors' own), but the paper never states whether those baselines were retrained on this dataset. (3) split_protocol coded not_reported: the 70/10/20 proportions are given but the partition method is never stated. (4) n_val/n_test not_reported: only n_train (16,800) is given as an integer. (5) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION worth flagging: the model 'was implemented in Raspberry Pi 3B+ to run on GPU mode' yet the Discussion says 'the current approach's incompatibility with edge devices presents a drawback'; no timing, power or throughput figure on the Pi is reported, so latency_measured_on_target_hw = no while target_hardware_named = Raspberry Pi 3B+. (6) 'false detection rate of 0.7%' is a per-detection rate, not a per-unit-time false alarm rate, so false_alarms_per_unit_time = not_reported.
